None: Um, so let's just go ahead and get started with your background. Maybe tell us a little bit about yourself.

Karthik Narasimhan: Sure, yeah. I'm a professor at Princeton. I've been here for seven years now. I work on broadly research around AI agents just to give a broad term here. But primarily around reinforcement learning and natural language processing, all that. Have been doing that for more than a decade now. I did my PhD back at MIT, and then spent a year at OpenAI. Which was just a really fun time because we actually co-authored the very first GPT paper back then, and it's been crazy to see how that's played out. And yeah, over after that I moved to Princeton. I also spent two years doing a sabbatical at Sierra, which is the new startup that's building agents for the enterprise.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. Um, so let's go ahead and start off, uh, way, way, way back when, um, in undergrad. Um, tell us a little about, about kinda your time at IIT Madras.

We learned not just things in AI but also, like, systems theory, all of that. So it was a, it was a really nice environment just to get, like, a very broad base. And I think one of the things that I really enjoyed was the AI classes obviously, and it was as an undergrad where you're very fascinated with programming and stuff, just thinking about machines automating lots of things is, was just, like, mind-blowing to me, right? And I still vividly remember the sort of, the one class that made me really super interested in AI was this intro to AI class taught by was it Bipa Kimani?

He's like a super senior prof. And we had this very nice, like, project where basically we had to build bots. Multiplayer sort of bots for the game of Snake. And it was, like, a whole competition and everything. So it was, like, a lot of fun just beating out other teams. Think, like 10, almost 15 years ago. Like you're building bots to play against each other and all that. But anyway, it was a lot of, a lot of fun. Made me wanna go deeper into AI and, yeah.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. Um, I guess, like, um, you know, IIT Madras is definitely a pretty hardworking place. Karthik Narasimhan: So the PhD is a very, very interesting time I must assure, like I mean folks who didn't even know, right? You know one of her prior students former students, like, Bronovan, he'd written, like, a really classic paper on, like, how you can use you know NLP to improve RL agents. Like, it's still, it's still to this day I consider one of the defining papers.

It sort of went under the radar, I feel, but, like, it basically taught a bot how to read the manual and play Civilization, which is, like, the coolest thing ever, which was the coolest thing I ever heard at that point for me. And yeah I went there. One of the things that I really had to learn from scratch was just, like just being proactive. Figuring out things on your own, being independent. I think I had all these qualities before, but, like, I cannot emphasize how important that is, right when you're a PhD student and you sort of want to make progress or, like, figure out your niche, right? So I think those, those things are probably far more important than your IQ level or, you know how how you, how you actually, like, how smart you are and things like that.

So anyway, so I think that was the PhD was a really rewarding experience. Started off working on some core NLP tasks. Things like information extraction and some kind of, like sentiment analysis, all that. But then very quickly I figured out my love for RL was still there, and this was actually because of I would credit my undergrad prof here, like, Ravindra, Professor Ravindra, and he's still at IIT Madras. Like, he taught this RL course which was, like, so interesting, so fascinating. So I kept thinking about RL, right? Right. Just like how you're doing or I'm doing as humans.

Karthik Narasimhan: I would consider myself an NLP person, go to NLP conferences and like, from the outside I'm, I was an NLP researcher, but inside really I just like, like I said, right? One of the, one of the first classes I took it was more about broadly about AI, right? And if I look back in hindsight, it's like even if you consider this whole grounding aspect to it. It's basically the feeling that I always had, like, language doesn't exist in isolation. So you shouldn't solve language in isolation, right? So I would say it's not really like a specific, like, pre-defined arc or something. Like, go from RL to this and this. The one guiding sort of principle I always try to, try to strive for is to try and basically push the envelope and define new areas.

You can sort of be really good at, like, empirical analysis and, like, have, like, really nice papers that showcase the different strengths and weaknesses. But I feel like the place that I'm most comfortable is, like, just trying to imagine one or two steps into the future and try to bring that and close the gap between what we're seeing now and that. And so that sort of, like, prompts you to be like, "Okay, what is useful in this real world-" kind of scenario. And all that. So I think SWE-Bench, TAO-Bench, those are sort of like even WebShop, I would say, like, those are sort of, like, pushing, trying to push towards, like, "Hey, let's not just get these systems to play Atari games." Which is cool. Which is great. But I think they are more capable than that, so let's go let's move past that.

Karthik Narasimhan: So I'd say when I guess when I started off there was a time of BERT, right? So BERT came out right after GPT, right? Then they took the bidirectional side of things. So I think it was pretty exciting even back then because it was kind of clear that using a transformer, you can go way further than LSTM which were the state of the art back then, right? So I think there was a whole line of looking at how pre-training is evolving. So if you recall, like, that was, that was when the whole pre-training thing evolved, right? Basically, like, you train it on a bunch of, like, raw text, and then you have these parameters that are initialized in such a nice way, right? So I think at that point, I would roughly categorize my interest as like, okay, figure out what's happening with pre-training.

How, how can this apply broadly, not just to NLP? And then the second was on, like, more fundamental problems around, like, RL, like the moral paper and other things where, like, trying to figure out what is missing in RL and what are things that can make it more practical, right? Because if you actually look at the sort of formalization of RL in the classic Sutton and Barto. It's great as a formalism in the theoretical sense. But a lot of things are not really practical, right? So, like, theoretically, yes, you will converge to the optimal policy, blah, blah, blah. But i- in reality, that's so, so far from what you wanna do, right? And for, in fact, for critical applications like, like training a robot. You can't have it destroy itself thousands of times, so. That was kind of the motivation towards what can you do to train these models safely using RL, POLCO, and all of that.

And then I think yeah, and then it was like as these models evolved, right, like the whole scaling paradigm had started. 2019, '20, '21. We were seeing two, three, even the BERT based models were expanding in size and all of that. So I think they were becoming increasingly capable. And it was reaching the point where and it was clear, more and more clear that some of the things that I had wanted to do even back in the PhD. So in text UK, IQN, you can actually think of as like a very rudimentary demonstration of an LLM based agent, right? So it's like it's used the language model to predict things, read text on the text games in RL. But it's, like, very, very rudimentary. It didn't work at all. Like it's like I mean, if you, if you look at that right now, you'll just laugh, right?

It's like, okay, what? But as these models get gone really powerful, right, you have this, like, LLM which has a lot of the right priors. A lot of things change, right? So RL, you don't assume any priors. But with an LLM, you have a lot of the right priors, a lot of the right heuristics. So you can actually do many of these things that we've always dreamt of doing, right? And so it was apparent to me, like, hey, we need to be able to, like, first off, put out the right benchmarks that need to, that need to really push these boundaries, right? So WebShop, for example, was one where, like, yeah, there's a really nice paper by folks at OpenAI. The mini world of this. But it was too rudimentary, too small again, right? So we were like, okay, take this, make it into a realistic task, like shop on Amazon.

Can these models do it, right? And they actually turned out they were not bad, right? So. So I'd say, like, most of the recent stuff for me has been not just to perform research in an isolation, but I think I would actually look at, like, what is something that can have impact. Doesn't have to have immediate impact, but even a few years down the line, right? Something that's more realistic. Let's push the boundaries here, and I think these models are incredibly smart, incredibly capable. I would say even right now, the benchmarks we have are probably a pretty low ceiling for these models. They can do so much more.

None: Hmm. Awesome. Um, you know, I think you worked on a lot of really amazing stuff during your time at Sierra. We built a few things internally and all of that, and then I think a few months down you know, we had a coffee chat, like Shenu was interning, and Noah, and Pedro, and I, and it was like kind of apparent that, hey this, this can be something that's not necessarily just an internal thing.

None: Mm-hmm. Awesome. And I guess like, I mean, these days, you know, we have, you know, SWE-bench. I think, uh, you know, more broadly, there's been a lot of other interesting benchmarks that have come out, right? Terminal Bench, and you already talked about Tau Bench. So there's this whole world of benchmarks. So I guess like maybe we'll start with like one question about benchmarks. Um, like how do you know your benchmark is a good benchmark? Like there's one argument that is like, okay, can your benchmark, like in a statistically significant way, separate out two different models and their capabilities? So if like every model is getting 100%, then obviously that's not a great benchmark. But like also, you know, say your benchmark is, you know, we want to evaluate tool use or tool calls, for instance. Um, or say for instance, you know, there is some qualitative characteristic that you want your benchmark to measure. Um, just because your benchmark statistically significantly, um, you know, separates two different models doesn't necessarily mean that it's separating them in the right way, AKA, that the benchmark is actually serving its intended qualitative purpose. And so there's like no real way to know what the answer is of how to build the right benchmark, 'cause there's no real way to know whether the benchmark you've constructed is the right benchmark. It's a different thing to say like, okay, you know, so model A and model B are both competing on the same benchmark. Model A does better than model B. But now the question is how do you construct a benchmark that is actually, you know, like it serves the purpose that it's intended to serve of what it's trying to model. And so it seems like you worked on a bunch of different benchmarks. I mean, like whether directly or indirectly, you have Tau Bench, we have SWE-bench. I'm sure there's infinite other benchmarks that your lab is about to come up with. So how do you think about it?

Karthik Narasimhan: So I think a benchmark can serve multiple purposes. And it's important to distinguish those purposes, I think. Right? So on the one hand, there is the quantitative aspect of it where like you sort of have a leaderboard and you could be like, "Oh, this model is number three, and this model is number two, and there's the gap of two points between them." I think that's useful as a ranking mechanism. There's a different purpose, right? The other purpose is also just to showcase a sort of task or a capability which is useful, and like you want the, you want the model to get better at that, right? Any model. It doesn't matter which model. You just want to climb to 100%, right? So I feel like people also look at benchmarks in one of these two angles, right?

To me, the more interesting angle is the second one, which is you feel like there's some capability that the model could have, but it's probably maybe currently lacking. Maybe it's not like all the way there, but you want to push the community towards like improving on that, right? And so I try to go for those, those kind of tasks where like it seems like- Hey, why are we not working on this thing? So a benchmark is a good way to sort of kickstart more community involvement there. I think ranking part is useful, right? Obviously, it's useful when you sort of benchmark your model against your competitor's model or somebody else's model. But beyond a certain point I don't think you wanna you know, wanna over-rotate on those results, right? Like, if you're at 20% and then you go up to, like, 80%, that's great.

You-- your model, that's a very clear signal. But if everyone's at 80% and you're climbing to 81 and 82 I mean, at that point there are all benchmarks get saturated, all benchmarks have issues. So at that point, it's probably worth your time to actually look at the next thing, right? So I think those are some principles in hindsight that I feel like they're worth, like thinking about.

Karthik Narasimhan: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah I think SWE-bench was and the SWE-agent harness, right? They were important in surfacing some of these things, right? Like, what's missing, right? You have these, like, strong models. They're clearly capable of writing good code. They're clearly capable of performing RAG. So I think the thing that just got highlighted was, like, okay, there are two gaps to solve. One was having the right harness. We call them as agent coding harnesses. Coding agent harnesses now. Basically giving them the right tools, the right ACI in some sense like agent computer interface. And second of all is just, like, training on more data that's specific for these coding tasks, right? Which is not just code but also the types of edits you wanna make and the file navigation, all that.

And I think we've seen both of them happen, right? So a lot of people have tried out different like, SWE-agent is one, Open Hands. Other people have tried out different things like A+. So it, it's great. Like, we've tried out very different things. We've learned lessons. And then the model building companies have taken this to heart as well. And they train the models on better data, specifically geared towards software engineering tasks and made them stronger there. So in that sense, I would say it's, like, it's exactly the thing that SWE-bench was aiming to do, right? Like, make it make us move from being like, "Okay, generate one function piece of code and then test it," to actually solving more realistic SWE, SWE tasks, right? So I think, yeah, having that sort of principle in mind is useful for any new benchmarks you use going forward.

reference:
Yeah. I think these are actually two different buckets, right? So— The continual learning part is almost like a problem that needs to be solved. There's not really a specific algorithm or anything. I mean continual learning, by the way, the problem space has existed for a few years now, right? At all the, like, big shot things. But I think the problem that needs to be solved, it's obvious why it needs to be solved. Because you can't be prompting the agent to do something and then expect it to just, like, continue to work in the same way forever. Like, you want it to be dynamic. You want it to learn from its mistakes. So I think this is a space where, like, maybe the, all the chatter is just because, like, it's, it has to be solved. It's, like, very, very obvious. Even take, for example customer service or yeah, right.

Like, you want these agents to learn and become better over time, right? This is actually something that Sierra's advantage is you know, you can actually do that with the data and all that. So I think it's an important thing. It's something everyone wants to solve. I don't think there's, like, a specific algorithm that's, like, the winner right now, or a specific method yet. But I suspect we'll see more of these crop, crop up. The RL for enterprises, I think it's a good it, it's a good idea in theory. But at the end of the day, RL is like a hammer. And you wanna be very, very clear on the problem you're using the hammer on, right? So that's something like at least from my experience at Sierra, it's like you only know that when you're deep into the problem, right?

Like, you need to have product knowledge or production causations, knowledge of everything that you can analyze the trajectories, all that. And that tells you where you need to do RL and all that. So it's kind of a... What I'm trying to say is, like, you want to be using RL for the right things, but you also need to have the whole setup— the environment, all of that. And that requires a lot more work than the actual RL piece, right? So— That's just my take now.

astra.text:
Yeah, I think on the RL side, the exciting thing is what we were talking about earlier, right? You're starting with a model that already has a lot of the right priors. So you don't have to learn everything from scratch. But I think the hard part is figuring out what you actually want to improve, and whether the environment you've created captures that.

Like, you can build an environment, build a verifier, and get the reward to go up. That's great. But does that translate to the agent being more useful when somebody actually interacts with it? That's the question, right? Especially in an enterprise, where you have different users, different policies, and things changing over time. Even within one task, there might be multiple ways to succeed. So I think a lot of the work is going to be in that connection between the training environment and the actual deployment. How do you get feedback from what happens in production, and how do you know that your next round of training actually addressed the problem?

And then continual learning, I think, is interesting because people mean slightly different things by it. Like, are you talking about updating the parameters of the model? Are you talking about an agent remembering something and using that memory the next time? From the perspective of the user, what you really want is for the system to get better as you work with it, right? If I've explained something to it yesterday, I don't want to have to explain the same thing again today.

So to me, the research question is, what should it retain from that experience? And how does it use that appropriately? Because something you learn in one situation might not apply in another. You also don't want learning something new to break something it was already doing well.

That's why I think these longer-horizon evaluations are really important. If you give the model one task and then reset everything, you're not really measuring any of this. But if you have it maintain a repository over two weeks, now you can ask: does it remember the decisions it made? Does it adapt when the requirements change? Does it keep making the same mistake? I think making those questions concrete would be really valuable. Then we can figure out which combination of memory, learning, and interaction actually helps.

sol.text:
Yeah, I think on the enterprise RL side, the phrase “create a verifier” makes the problem sound much cleaner than it usually is. In coding, you can run tests and get a relatively crisp signal. In an enterprise setting, what is the reward? Is it that the customer’s issue was resolved, that they were satisfied, that the company followed policy, or that the interaction was efficient? Those can conflict, and some of the consequences only become visible much later. So the hard part is often not the RL algorithm. It’s specifying the objective, collecting reliable feedback, and building an environment that is sufficiently representative of production.

And then you have the safety issue, right? Traditional RL assumes you can explore and make mistakes. But you cannot have an enterprise agent experimenting on real customers by issuing refunds incorrectly or violating policy thousands of times. So you need good simulators, offline data, careful constraints, and really strong evals before anything reaches production. But simulators also have gaps, and the agent can learn to exploit those gaps rather than become better at the real task. I think a lot of startups will discover that the infrastructure and evaluation work is much larger than simply putting an RL loop around an LLM.

Continual learning is related, but I think people use that phrase to mean several different things. Sometimes they mean giving the model memory or retrieval so it can use information from previous interactions. Sometimes they mean updating the model’s parameters continuously. And sometimes they mean that an agent should adapt its strategy as the environment, the user, or the organization changes. Those are different problems, and we should be precise about which one we’re solving.

The really exciting version to me is an agent operating over a long horizon, learning from its interactions, and improving without forgetting what it already knows or picking up undesirable behavior. That brings in memory, credit assignment, nonstationarity, and deciding what should actually be learned. If one interaction goes badly, should the model update itself? Probably not immediately. So you need mechanisms for aggregating evidence, attributing outcomes to the right decisions, and making updates that are both fast and safe.

And this comes back to benchmarks. Static datasets are not going to be sufficient for continual learning. You need dynamic environments where the task changes, information arrives over time, and performance is measured across weeks or many interactions—not just on one episode. That’s what I’m most excited about: longer-horizon agents that don’t merely complete a task once, but can maintain something, adapt to people and environments, and demonstrably get better through experience.

opus.text:
Yeah, I mean, so the RL for enterprise thing, I think the, the honest answer is that the hard part is not the RL, right? Like, the algorithms, we, we sort of know what to do. PPO, GRPO, whatever flavor you want. The hard part is the environment and the verifier. And I think people underestimate that by, like, an order of magnitude. Because in coding you kind of got lucky, right? The test suite is your verifier. It comes for free. Somebody else wrote it. But if you go to, like, a customer support setting or, like, an internal operations workflow at some company, what is the reward, right? Did the customer come away happy? You find that out three days later, maybe, if they fill out a survey. So it's noisy, it's delayed, it's partially observable, and half the time the thing you can actually measure is a proxy for the thing you care about. And then the classic RL lesson kicks in, which is the agent will absolutely exploit that gap. Like, reward hacking is not a new failure mode, we've been seeing it in RL for, for decades, right? So I think a lot of those startups are gonna discover that they're actually environment-building companies and, and simulation companies, which is mostly software engineering, not research. Which is fine, but it's a different business than the one people think they're in.

On continual learning, I, I'd say first we should be careful because people mean, like, four different things by it, right? Some people mean memory, like retrieval and, and a scratchpad. Some people mean actually updating weights online. Some people mean personalization. To me the interesting version is the one where the agent does a task, screws up, and is meaningfully better at it the next week. Because right now every session basically starts with amnesia, right? You have this incredibly smart thing that has no idea it failed at exactly this yesterday.

And the problems there are, are genuinely hard. It's credit assignment over really long horizons, it's deciding what to retain and what to throw away, which is a, sort of a value judgment, not just a compression problem. And then forgetting, obviously.

But the thing I keep coming back to is we don't have evals for it. Like, every benchmark we have is a static snapshot, you run the model through it, you get a number. That tells you nothing about whether a system improves over time. So, you know, going back to what we were saying earlier about dynamic evals, I think whoever builds the right eval for continual learning does the field a bigger favor than whoever builds the first method. And that's probably the thing I'm most interested in poking at.

grok.text:
Yeah, yeah. So I think, I mean, starting with the RL-for-enterprises piece, because that’s the one I’ve lived in the most, right? I think the pitch sounds almost too clean. You build a verifier, you wrap the company’s tools into an environment, you run RL, and suddenly you have a specialist agent. And look, conceptually I love that. I’ve been in RL for more than a decade. But the gap between that story and actually doing it is pretty large.

The first thing people are going to hit is that the verifier is the product, not the algorithm. In coding, you get lucky, right? You can run tests. In math, there’s a ground truth. The moment you go into customer support, ops, anything like what we were doing at Sierra, “correct” is messy. It’s multi-objective. Did you follow policy? Did you actually resolve the issue? Did you not invent a refund the company doesn’t allow? Was the user happy? Did you take too many turns? We had a paper on multi-objective RL back in 2019, and I still think that problem is very much alive. You don’t get a nice scalar reward you can just optimize. If your verifier is noisy or incomplete, RL will happily exploit it, and you’ll train a policy that looks great on paper and is terrible in production.

The second thing is you cannot learn the way classic RL wants you to learn. I keep coming back to this. Sutton and Barto is a beautiful formalism, but you cannot have the agent fail in front of real customers a thousand times. You can’t have a robot destroy itself. Same thing here. So sample efficiency, safety, being able to do most of the learning in some kind of sandbox — that’s still hard. And this is where the user simulation stuff from Tau Bench actually matters a lot. If you can simulate users with high fidelity, maybe you get a training loop that isn’t just burning production traffic. If you can’t, I think a lot of these startups are going to discover that the environment they built is a toy, and the real enterprise is this partially observed, constantly changing thing with messy APIs and policies that shift every quarter.

And then, honestly, evals. I still remember week one at Sierra, Brett was like, we need to get evals right. Before RL, before anything. Because if you don’t know how to measure success in that workflow, you’re just optimizing noise. I think that’s going to be the unsexy bottleneck. People will have a nice algorithm and a nice environment, and then they’ll realize they don’t actually know what “good” means for this particular customer.

On continual learning — yeah, I think this is the real one, and it’s connected to what I was saying about long-horizon tasks. Right now most agents are basically smart in a session and then they forget. Or they have some retrieval memory that’s pretty crude. But a real coworker gets better over weeks. They learn this codebase, this customer, this set of policies. That’s continual learning.

I think the research is going to split into a few threads. One is memory — not just stuffing more into the context window, but actually storing and retrieving the right experiences. Two is updating something online, whether that’s the model or some adapter or some memory module, without catastrophic forgetting, without breaking the things it already knows. That’s an old problem, but it’s showing up in a very practical way now. And three, which I think people underweight, is evaluation. Static datasets do not capture this at all. You need the world to shift, the user to shift, and then you measure whether the agent adapted. Those dynamic evals we were talking about — user simulators, dual-control environments, even competitive setups like what John is doing with Code Clash — that’s how you even know continual learning is happening.

What I’m excited about is an agent that can sit with a repository for two weeks, or with a customer for two months, and actually get better because it lived there. Not because you did a big offline fine-tune. That’s closer to how humans work, and I think that’s a lot of the remaining gap between models that are incredibly capable in a single shot and systems you’d actually trust as a coworker. The models already have a lot of the right priors, which is the thing RL never had. The question is whether we can keep those priors and still let the system keep learning. That’s the part I want us to figure out.

gemini.text:
Yeah, I mean, starting with the RL for enterprise side, I think the biggest challenge—and we kind of touched on this earlier—is really the verifier and the reward signal, right? In games or coding tasks like SWE-bench, you have a compiler or you have unit tests. It’s very discrete, and you can easily verify whether something succeeded or failed. But in enterprise workflows, what does success actually look like? It’s often super nuanced, subjective, and dependent on shifting company policies. And like I mentioned earlier with things like safe RL, you can’t just let an agent explore randomly and break production databases or mess up real customer interactions thousands of times to learn an optimal policy. So creating high-fidelity simulators, reliable verifiers, and safe environments where you don't fall victim to reward hacking is going to be a huge hurdle for a lot of these enterprise RL setups.

And then on the continual learning front, I think it’s super exciting because right now, our models are essentially amnesiacs, right? You deploy a model, and every conversation or interaction basically starts from a clean slate unless you put things into the context window with RAG. But context stuffing is not true continual learning. True continual learning is about: how do you actually adapt your model over time from feedback and experience without catastrophic forgetting? How do you ensure that when an agent learns a new rule or workflow today, it doesn't completely overwrite or break everything it was doing well yesterday? 

So I think research there is going to have to look at better hybrid architectures—combining parametric updates with fast, dynamic non-parametric memory—and figuring out how agents can learn from their own mistakes over weeks and months of deployment. If we really want long-horizon agents that can maintain a repository or act as a long-term collaborator, continual learning isn't just a buzzword; it's really the fundamental piece that we have to solve next.

kimi.text:
Yeah, so on the RL for enterprise side, I think the hype is real but the gap between the hype and the reality is also real. A lot of these startups are like, "Okay, build a verifier, build an environment, RL your way to a great agent." And I think the thing that's easy to underestimate is just how hard it is to build the right environment and the right verifier for a real enterprise workflow, right? Like, in academia we have the luxury of clean tasks. But in a real company, the state of the world is messy. There's a long tail of edge cases, the APIs are half-documented, the policies are written down in some PDF somewhere. And if your verifier is even slightly off, these models will reward hack the hell out of it. They're very, very good at finding the loophole in your reward, right?

And the second thing is just stakes. I mentioned this before with the robot, right? You can't have it destroy itself a thousand times. Same thing with an enterprise agent. You can't have it mess up a thousand customer interactions before it learns something. So you need simulators with really high fidelity, which kind of goes back to the whole Tau Bench philosophy, right? Simulate the user, simulate the environment well enough that you can actually train there. And that's genuinely hard. So I think the companies that succeed will be the ones that invest in evals first, before the RL. That was literally lesson number one at Sierra. If your eval is wrong, everything downstream is wrong.

On continual learning, yeah, I'm excited about it. I think there are a few big open questions. One is just, like, where does the learning actually live? Is it in the weights? Is it in some kind of external memory or context? There's a spectrum there, and I don't think we've figured out the right point on it. There's this classic tradeoff between stability and plasticity, catastrophic forgetting and all that, which has been around for decades. But now it's not a theory problem anymore, it's like an actual deployment problem, which makes it exciting.

And I think the evals angle matters here too. Continual learning is fundamentally a dynamic thing, so the static dataset paradigm breaks down even harder. Like, how do you even measure whether a system got better over two weeks of deployment? You need the dynamic, simulation-based evals we were just talking about. So I think the research is gonna look like better memory architectures, more sample-efficient online learning, and new evals that can track learning over long horizons. And honestly, all three of these things, the RL-for-enterprise stuff, continual learning, the eval stuff, they're all converging on the same picture, which is agents that live in the world for a long time and keep getting better. That's ultimately what I'm excited about.

fable.text:
Yeah, so, okay, let me take the RL for enterprises one first, because I think that's the one where I've, like, actually seen it from the inside a bit, right? So the pitch is basically, like, "Hey, RL works for math, it works for code, because you have a verifier. So let's go build verifiers for every enterprise task and then just do RL on it," right? And I think that's directionally right. Like, I do believe that. But I think people underestimate how much of the work is in the environment and the reward and not in the RL, right? Like, the RL algorithm at this point is, is like, is kind of a commodity almost. So the hard part is, like, what is the reward signal for, "Did this agent handle this customer's refund correctly according to this company's policy that changed last Tuesday," right? It's not a unit test. It's, like, a fuzzy thing. It's a long horizon thing. It has all these constraints that are, like, half written down and half in someone's head. And if you get the reward slightly wrong, the model will find it, right? Like, that's the one thing we know for sure from a decade of RL. It will exploit whatever hole you leave in there. So I think, honestly, like, building a good environment for an enterprise is kind of like building the product. Like, that's what we learned at Sierra. The evals and the environment, it's not a side thing, it's the core thing. And so if you're a startup and you think you're just gonna, like, wrap a verifier around somebody's workflow and hand it to a model company, I think the question is, like, where does the value accrue, right? Because the environment kind of encodes the domain knowledge, and once the model has been trained on it, like, what's left? So I think the ones that'll do well are the ones that are really close to the actual data and the actual outcomes and can keep updating the reward as the world changes, not the ones that just build a static gym and, like, sell it once.

And then the continual learning thing, I mean, it's funny, right? Because if you go back to Sutton and Barto, like the whole formalism is an agent living in an environment for a long time and getting better from experience. That's, like, what RL was supposed to be from the start. And then we kind of, like, threw all of that away and said, "Okay, let's pre-train a giant model, freeze it, and then it's frozen forever," right? So, so in some sense, I see it as us coming back around to the original problem, but now with a model that actually has the priors to make it work. So I think the research questions there are actually pretty fundamental. Like, one, what is the unit of learning? Is it the weights, is it the context, is it some external memory thing that you read and write to? Right now, honestly, the most practical version of continual learning is just a really long context window and some retrieval, right? And that works surprisingly well, but it's, it's clearly not the whole story. Two, the forgetting problem is real. Like, catastrophic forgetting didn't go away because the models got bigger. And three, which is the one I keep coming back to, is how do you even evaluate it, right? Like, this ties back to what we were saying earlier. All of our benchmarks are static. You run the model once, you get a number. For continual learning, the whole point is that the number should go up over time, on the same task, as the agent accumulates experience. So you need evals that are, like, two weeks long instead of two minutes long. And nobody really has those yet. So I think that's actually where I'm excited, like, less on the "let's invent a new gradient update rule" side, and more on, like, can we actually build the environments and the evals where an agent has to, like, maintain something, adapt to changes, remember what it did last week and not repeat the mistakes, right? Because I think once you can measure that properly, the methods will follow. That's kind of been the pattern every single time, right?

r011.rationale: It says effective enterprise RL depends on the real product, production outcomes, company-specific policies, domain knowledge, and the surrounding environment.
